Gamja Jorim Soy-Braised Potatoes

Gamja jorim is the banchan that converts potato people on first bite: small chunks braised in soy, sugar, and garlic until the edges caramelize and glaze and the interiors drink the braise.

Korean · Easy · Serves 4–6 as banchan

Behind the dish

A PLACE AT
the table.

Stream: heritage — the caramelized braise. Gamja jorim is the banchan that converts potato people on first bite: small chunks braised in soy, sugar, and garlic until the edges caramelize and glaze and the interiors drink the braise. It sits beside the grill's meats doing carbohydrate duty with a fork-sweetness that rice never attempts — the children's champion and the adults' quiet favorite of the banchan board. The whole technique is a reduced braise with corn syrup's gloss, finished fast.

The potatoes
The braise

Set yourself up

Before you cook

  • Even 3 cm chunks, and rinse them once after cutting — the rinse takes the surface starch that would make the braise gluey, leaving the starch that makes it cling.
  • Measure everything before the pot gets hot: this braise moves from simmered to glazed in the last five minutes and wants no measuring pauses.

LET’S make it.

  1. 01
    Oil and garlic in a wide pan over medium until the garlic just turns blond (30 seconds — blond, not brown; browned garlic runs bitter through a sweet braise), potatoes in, stirred to coat, 2 minutes of sizzling together. Checkpoint — the potato edges turn translucent-gold and the pan smells of toasted garlic — the braise's flavor floor just got laid.
  2. 02
    Water, soy, corn syrup, and sugar in; stir, lid on, medium-low. Ten minutes at a gentle bubble, stirring once at the halfway mark. Checkpoint — a paring knife into the largest chunk slides in with no resistance — the potato is cooked, and everything from here is reduction, not cooking. If the knife catches, three more minutes, lid on.
  3. 03
    Lid off, and the reduction — the technique. High-medium now, stirring and turning every 60–90 seconds as the liquid boils down. The braise goes from soupy to syrupy to glaze: the pan's liquids thicken, the sugars caramelize on the turned potato faces, and the potatoes bounce in a slow thick sizzle instead of a boil. Five to six minutes, off the heat the moment the glaze coats and the pan is nearly dry. Checkpoint — a test chunk: glazed dark at two or three faces, glossy, and it holds its shape but yields to the tooth — the braise has painted it, not dissolved it. Burnt-sugar smell is the one-second warning: off the heat now, not next stir. Sesame oil, seeds, scallion over, off the heat. Chef’s Note — corn syrup versus honey is this record's honest fork: corn syrup (the Korean home default) gives the glassy, no-flavor glaze that lets soy and garlic lead; honey gives flavor and browns faster and runs a shade softer. Either works — the clock in step 3 shortens by a minute with honey. What does not work is sugar alone: it crystallizes grainy instead of glossing, and the glaze is half the dish.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
Glaze burnt bitterWalked away in the reduction60–90 second turns; off at the smell
Potatoes fell apartOver-stirred or floury potatoesWaxy yellow/red, gentle turns
Glaze thin, soupyReduction stopped earlyThe pan should be nearly dry before the finish
One-note sweetSoy under-runA teaspoon more soy at the taste

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

  • Keeps 3 days refrigerated and reheats beautifully (pan, medium, 3 minutes, a splash of water to loosen the glaze) — the make-ahead banchan par excellence, arguably better on day two.
  • Variations: the same braise on lotus root (#B18) and on quail eggs (#B19); a chili half in the braise for the drinking table; day-after glazed potatoes beside a fried egg is the lunchbox classic.
